But sizable numbers of Latino voters are unhappy, especially those personally fearful about ICE or those who know someone who has been deported or detained. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The latest NBC News/Telemundo poll shows 65% of Latino voters have negative views of ICE, compared to 28% who have positive views. When it comes to Customs and Border Protection, 46% view the agency negatively, compared to 34% who view it positively. The survey also shows: → 69% of Latino voters disapprove of Trump’s approach to immigration, and two-thirds say his enforcement operations have gone too far. → An overwhelming 83% said they do support deporting undocumented immigrants who have committed serious crimes, but 60% oppose deportations of all undocumented immigrants currently in the country. → Notably, 18% of Latino voters say they or someone close to them has strongly considered leaving the country. articles.title: School protests, blockades resume in France despite PM’s promise to act
articles.summary: Dozens of people have been injured in the protests, including students, teachers, and police officers.
articles.body:
Protests have resumed at schools across France as high school students press on with demands for more education funding and better conditions, the day after the country’s prime minister ordered ministers to provide an action plan.

Reporting from Paris, Al Jazeera’s Natacha Butler said university students and more trade unions have joined the nationwide protests and that a large rally is expected in the capital on Thursday.

“They are moving around, trying to block off the streets,” Butler said from outside one school, where university students were barricading a large area.

“They are out, they say, in solidarity with high school students because they say it’s important that as many young people join in the protests as possible,” she added.

The wave of protests began in a high school in a deprived area of Paris on September 21 . Tens of thousands of students across the country have since marched with a range of demands, from renovated school buildings to fewer classroom hours.

Rights groups have accused security officials of using disproportionate force against protesters.

Several demonstrators have been injured, including one teenager who lost a hand and another whose jaw was shattered by an exploding stun grenade. They have since been banned at marches.

Police officers and teachers have also been injured, authorities say, accusing students of committing violent acts. At least 6,600 arrests – mostly of minors – have been made so far, according to the Interior Ministry.

Authorities said 375 schools were either fully or partially closed on Thursday, and that two dozen had been burned or destroyed.

The demonstrations are increasing pressure on the cash-strapped outgoing government of Emmanuel Macron ahead of April elections.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu condemned the violence in a TV address on Wednesday. He faulted “political leaders who use this anger to conduct their electoral battles”, after opposition leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon called for protesters to keep marching.

Lecornu has ordered ministers to provide an action plan responding to students’ demands by the end of the month, but protesters remain unconvinced.

“As far as they are concerned, the government only talks about solutions but never actually comes up with concrete actions, so they say they are going to keep coming out onto the streets until their demands are met,” Butler said.

articles.title: ‘Let them hit Los Angeles’: Trump clarifies Iran war remarks, says he ‘won’t let that happen’
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump sought to clarify his controversial remarks about Iran attacking Los Angeles and San Diego at a Texas campaign rally on
articles.body: US President Donald Trump sought to clarify his controversial remarks about Iran attacking Los Angeles and San Diego at a Texas campaign rally on Wednesday, saying the US would “not let that happen” as he campaigned for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections.Trump had sparked a backlash earlier this week after suggesting that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego while discussing the threat posed by a nuclear-armed Iran at a rally in Nebraska.At a rally in San Antonio on Wednesday, Trump again referred to the possibility of Iran firing a missile at the two California cities, but said the US would prevent such a scenario.“You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles if you want to see some bad things happen,” Trump said. “You want to see a country that would be in free fall?”“We’re not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. We’re not letting that happen,” he added.Trump’s original comments had drawn sharp criticism from California Democrats. Governor Gavin Newsom accused the president of being “deranged and dangerous”, while Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass said the remarks could potentially compromise the safety of the city.Bass said she may ask Congress to investigate Trump’s comments, according to NBC News. San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also pushed back against the remarks, saying the city was “not collateral damage”.The White House defended Trump, saying his comments had been misrepresented. White House communications director Steven Cheung said Trump was referring to what could have happened if Iran had developed nuclear weapons.Trump made the remarks during a rally aimed at boosting Texas Republicans ahead of the midterm elections. He campaigned for attorney general Ken Paxton, who is running for the Senate against Democrat James Talarico.The rally also reflected the political tensions surrounding Trump as Republicans prepare for the midterms. The president was repeatedly interrupted by protesters during his nearly two-hour speech.Trump also announced that former MLB pitcher Roger Clemens would receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom, calling the former seven-time Cy Young Award winner deserving of the honour.You use AI every day. articles.title: 'Will be doing injustice to my alliance partners': Chirag Paswan says his party has identified 'A' category seats for UP polls
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan said that his Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) has identified its priority and 'A' category seats in Uttar Pradesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Union minister Chirag Paswan said that his Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) has identified its priority and 'A' category seats in Uttar Pradesh and has a clear idea of the minimum number of constituencies it wants to contest as part of an alliance.Chirag Paswan, whose party is part of the BJP-led NDA, did not disclose the number of seats it is seeking. He said that doing so at this stage would be unfair to its alliance partners.“If I share those figures publicly at this stage, I would be doing an injustice to my alliance partners. Within the party, we are very clear and focused about which seats should be our priority. We have also identified the 'A' category seats, as we call them in political terminology, and we have a clear idea of the minimum number of seats our party would like to contest as part of the alliance...”The statement comes as the LJP (Ram Vilas) looks to establish its electoral presence in Uttar Pradesh while remaining aligned with the BJP-led alliance. Chirag has indicated that contesting as part of the alliance is the party's priority, although he has kept open the option of fighting independently.The LJP (Ram Vilas) leader highlighted his belief that voters benefit when they have more political choices. He suggested that his party could present itself as an alternative if an alliance is not formed.“Look, I believe in democracy. The more alternatives there are, the stronger democracy is. The more options people have to choose, the stronger democracy is,” he said, “Democracy is strong. In such a situation, if there is no conflict, as an alternative, I will definitely present myself. Ultimately, this decision has to be taken by the people of Uttar Pradesh.”At the same time, Paswan stressed that the party's preference is to contest with its alliance partners. He pointed to the arrangements in Bihar, Jharkhand and Delhi.“In such a situation, we are definitely in the priority centre in the alliance. We are in the alliance in Bihar. We fought the elections in the alliance in Jharkhand,” Chirag said, “We fought the elections in Delhi. The priority will definitely be that we fight the elections under the same alliance. But this alliance was mainly prepared for the centre and Bihar.”He said the party has also contested independently in states where there is no alliance arrangement, citing Nagaland as an example.“In other states, like we fought the elections alone in Nagaland. My two MLA's are also in Nagaland. In such a situation, we have the freedom in other states.”On Uttar Pradesh, he said the party would make an effort to reach an alliance agreement but could contest alone if that does not happen.“Even if we could not form an alliance, we can fight the elections alone. But yes, there will definitely be an effort. But I think it is too early to comment. “As the elections are coming closer, there will be more clarity on these things.”Chirag Paswan pointed to his commitment to stay in alliance during the 2020 Bihar assembly elections citing his commitment to Prime Minister Narendra Modi.He said, “For me, such a moment came in 2020, immediately after the death of my leader and father Ram Vilas Paswan ji, when we could not form an alliance in Bihar. But my dedication to my Prime Minister was so great that I did not go to any alternative alliance. I fought the elections alone.”He added, “A large population of Bihar supported us. More than 6% support. We met there, who gave my party that seriousness”Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: A Maryland DoorDash driver’s brakes failed and his car was totalled during a delivery, yet he still told the customer where to collect the food; the video went viral and his fundraiser later climbed past $15,000
articles.summary: A DoorDash delivery driver in Maryland has become a hero after he delivered food to the customer despite being involved in a serious car accident.
articles.body: A DoorDash delivery driver in Maryland has become a hero after he delivered food to the customer despite being involved in a serious car accident. The driver's brakes failed and his car got completely damaged, but he still contacted his customer and offered to let him collect the order from the accident scene. The customer recorded the unusual pickup, and the video soon went viral online. An fundraiser was also launched to help the driver replace his car and cover medical expenses.The driver, identified as William Koroma, was making his last delivery of the night on Church Road in Bowie, Maryland, when the accident occurred, Fox News reported last month. According to Koroma, his vehicle suffered brake failure, resulting in a major crash. He survived the accident and later said that no one else was seriously injured.Despite what had happened, Koroma contacted his customer, Glenn Ndibnu, to explain why he could not complete the delivery. Instead of simply cancelling the order, he told Ndibnu that he could come to the crash site and collect his food if he wanted.Ndibnu decided to go to the location and began recording as he approached the scene. Several emergency vehicles were present, with their lights flashing. Koroma's badly damaged car was visible nearby, while the customer's food order had been placed on the pavement. The video captured Ndibnu's surprise at finding himself collecting a food delivery from the scene of a serious accident.The unusual food pickup In the video, Ndibnu explained how he had ended up at the location after receiving a message from his delivery driver. "I DoorDashed some food, and my DoorDasher told me he got in a car accident, and he was like, ‘I can come meet him and get the food from him,'" he said as quoted by Fox News.As he approached the crash site, Ndibnu spotted what appeared to be his order on the pavement. However, he also appeared uncomfortable about collecting his food while the driver was dealing with the aftermath of the accident.He eventually walked over to collect the order. Before leaving, he apologised to Koroma and checked whether he was alright.The footage was subsequently shared on social media and attracted widespread attention. The attention also brought Koroma's circumstances into focus. The accident had left the driver facing several financial difficulties.William's recovery and transportation fundFollowing the crash, Koroma started a GoFundMe campaign titled "William's Recovery and Transportation Fund" to raise money for another vehicle and other essential expenses.In his appeal, he explained that the accident happened while he was working on his final DoorDash delivery of the night."My vehicle experienced brake failure, and I was involved in a major accident. My car was totaled, and I am deeply grateful that I survived and that no one else was seriously injured," Koroma wrote.Koroma said the loss of his vehicle had affected his ability to travel and work. He also revealed that he had lost his job after the accident."Since the accident, I have been facing several challenges at once. Losing my vehicle has left me without reliable transportation, and I have also lost my job," he said.According to his fundraising appeal, the situation has made it difficult for him to manage everyday expenses, including food and other basic necessities. Koroma also said he was dealing with medical costs resulting from the accident.Fundraiser crosses $16,000 As the video gained attention, Ndibnu shared a link to Koroma's fundraiser through his Instagram posts, allowing people who had watched the footage to contribute.The latest GoFundMe page shows that the campaign has collected $16,595 from 850 donations, against an updated target of $18,000.Koroma explained that the donations would primarily help him purchase another vehicle, allowing him to regain reliable transportation. Part of the money would also go towards medical bills and urgent living expenses.He said having a vehicle again would be an important step towards returning to work and improving his financial situation.In his appeal, Koroma thanked those supporting him and encouraged people who could not donate to share the fundraiser with others.You use AI every day. articles.title: Residents airlifted to safety in central Chile as El Niño blamed for torrential rains
articles.summary: The Mapocho river has burst its banks after an unusually large amount of rain fell in recent days.
articles.body:
Police in central Chile have airlifted several residents to safety after rising floodwaters left them trapped in their homes.

Recent torrential rains caused the Mapocho river to burst its banks, flooding large parts of the city of Talagante, 35km (22 miles) south-west of the capital, Santiago.

Santiago has seen 74mm of rainfall in the first seven days of this month, making it the rainiest October for the area in 76 years, meteorologists have said.

They have warned that this year's unusually strong El Niño climate phenomenon will likely continue to bring unusually wet weather, powerful winds and storms to the region during the southern hemisphere's spring.

Officials said one person had been found dead in a flooded underpass in the city of San Bernardo, south of Santiago, although they have yet to confirm the cause of death.

In Talagante, police used helicopters to rescue people and pets living on the banks of the Mapocho who had been surprised by the fast-rising waters overnight.

Dirt roads turned into rivers in the riverside community which, unlike in July's storms, had not been evacuated ahead of the heavy downpours.

Climate experts have warned that the 2026-2027 El Niño is likely to cause major shifts in weather patterns around the world, intensifying droughts in some areas and floods in others.

In central Chile, it is expected to trigger above-average rainfall.

articles.title: Russian strike kills at least 33 in eastern Ukraine in deadliest single attack this year
articles.summary: At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, marking the deadliest attack from a single strike this year.
articles.body: At least 33 people were killed on Thursday when a Russian strike caused two public buses to catch fire in eastern Ukraine, local authorities said, marking the deadliest attack from a single strike this year. Another 18 people were injured in the attack in Kramatorsk, a city in the Donetsk region, which prompted authorities there to shut down the public transport system and urge people to move to safer parts of the country. “The Russians are deliberately targeting civilians,” said Vadym Filashkin, the head of the Donetsk regional military administration. “For them, a bus full of passengers is an attractive target precisely because a single strike can kill as many people as possible.” The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (SES) said the Russian strike caused a fire on two buses and in the surrounding area. Rescue workers were at the scene to help survivors and extinguish the blaze, the SES added. Filashkin said he had ordered the suspension of public transportation in the cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk in the wake of the attack and called on civilians to move to safer areas. “I urge everyone who remains in the Donetsk region to evacuate to safer regions of Ukraine,” he said. “Russia is bringing death to Ukrainian soil. It is striking our cities, killing our people, and multiplying its crimes every day,” added Filashkin as he offered his condolences to the families and loved ones of victims. A mass Russian missile attack on Kyiv in July killed 33 people across the city in a coordinated barrage. Yet Thursday’s attack marks the highest death toll this year from a single strike. Both Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are crucial industrial cities close to the front line. Together with nearby Kostiantynivka and Druzhkivka, they form the core of Ukraine’s remaining “fortress belt” in the Donetsk region. Kramatorsk has long served as a strategic rear point for the Ukrainian units serving along the eastern front – and as a place to which exhausted troops could retreat for a few days of rest before their next mission. But a press officer with Ukraine’s 93rd mechanized brigade told CNN last month that is no longer an option due to frequent shelling. The fortress belt has slowly eroded over the past four and a half years. Its southernmost anchor, Kostyantynivka, has now been effectively lost as a stronghold.

articles.title: India to Turkiye, can new proposals to broker Russia-Ukraine truce succeed?
articles.summary: India, Turkiye, Egypt and the US have put forward proposals for ceasefires in bid to protect global energy and shipping.
articles.body:
Ukraine says it has received proposals from India, Turkiye, Egypt and the United States to broker talks with Russia. The offers come as the two adversaries escalate attacks on each other’s energy and port infrastructure with their war now in its fifth year.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha revealed the four proposals at a briefing in Kyiv on Friday and singled out New Delhi’s. “The most comprehensive is India’s proposal,” he said, adding that India had signalled a willingness to play a role for the first time.

None of the proposals aims to end the war. Each seeks a narrower truce, covering energy facilities, ports or commercial shipping in the Black Sea.

India has not made its plan public. Quoting unnamed sources, however, Indian media have reported it has three parts. According to the Hindustan Times, it would aim to protect infrastructure, keep grain and energy supplies moving through Black Sea ports, and ensure the safety of commercial shipping.

The first part – mutually halting strikes on energy facilities and ports – matches what Kyiv has been demanding. Sybiha said any deal must be a complete energy truce that covers port infrastructure as well.

The second part builds on the Black Sea Grain Initiative , which Turkiye and the United Nations mediated in 2022 but Russia abandoned in 2023.

The third part, protecting merchant ships and their crews, is particularly important to India because Indian sailors have been killed or harmed on Black Sea routes .

The sources were quoted as saying India’s plan goes further than the other three proposals because it covers infrastructure and shipping together. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that it incorporates elements of the Turkish, Egyptian and US initiatives. The Kyiv Post reported that Sybiha also described the plan as addressing a possible ceasefire along the front lines, although other accounts said he gave no specifics.

The proposal likely took shape during Indian External Affairs Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar’s first visit to Ukraine last month and in a later meeting with Sybiha at the UN General Assembly in New York, also in September. Jaishankar said New Delhi was “trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue”.

What do we know about the Turkish and Egyptian proposals?

Very little. Neither Ankara nor Cairo has published details. Both reportedly focus on keeping Black Sea grain supplies moving by suspending attacks on commercial shipping. Some reports said the two countries proposed a grain truce jointly while others described two separate plans.

Turkiye has done this before. With the UN, it steered the 2022 grain deal, one of the few narrow truces of the war to hold for any length of time. Ankara and the UN are now organising new Black Sea talks with a round planned for October.

Beyond its Black Sea focus, almost nothing is known about Egypt’s proposal. Its interest, however, is clear: Egypt relies on Ukraine for nearly one-third of its grain supplies.

According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Washington has proposed three steps: a mutual halt to energy strikes, a reopening of the grain corridor and a trilateral meeting with Ukraine and Russia, possibly in Abu Dhabi.

The latest effort began in early September when US President Donald Trump’s envoys visited Kyiv and Moscow and secured an agreement in principle for a trilateral meeting. Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on September 5 while Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the US twice in September.

The trilateral meeting has since been pushed back. It had been expected to take place in the United Arab Emirates in early October. Washington now wants it in late October, and people close to the talks blamed the delay on Russia.

Washington has also invited Putin to the Group of 20 summit in Miami, Florida, in December. “We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said. The Kremlin said no decision has been made.

At the same time, the US is applying pressure to try to end the war. Trump recently signed a law giving him sweeping powers to sanction buyers of Russian energy.

He has also called on Ukraine to stop targeting Russian diesel facilities amid a diesel prices crisis in the US, where Trump faces tricky midterm elections next month. “Mr Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” he said on September 13. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.” This drew much criticism that Trump instead should focus his comments on Russia, which began the war with its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

He is reportedly sceptical about his own government’s latest diplomatic initiative. People familiar with his thinking have told US media that he doubted Putin would agree to an energy truce before winter.

Sybiha said Ukraine would agree to a truce but with conditions. It would accept an energy and Black Sea shipping ceasefire, but only as a combined package, he said.

He added that Kyiv is also open to an unconditional ceasefire along the current front lines. Zelenskyy backs the US-proposed meeting but stressed it needs “not only Ukraine but also the Russian side” to support it.

Moscow has been warm in tone but has committed to nothing. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia would welcome India’s peace efforts while Putin said Modi has “very good ideas aimed at finding mutually acceptable solutions”, but he did not elaborate.

In private, Moscow appears to have said no. A Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that Russia has rejected India’s proposal although this has not been confirmed publicly. Ukraine’s agriculture minister said Russia had rejected every Black Sea ceasefire option the mediators have presented.

Why are Global South countries becoming more involved?

Food supplies, the lives of their citizens and fuel prices are all at stake.

“I think it’s clear to many countries that this war is not a localised war, but it’s a war that has these global consequences,” Fredrik Wesslau, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, told Al Jazeera.

Russia and Ukraine account for more than a quarter of global wheat shipments, and their attacks on each other’s ports helped push wheat futures to a three-year high in August.

Sailors from countries with no links to the war are being killed. At least five Indian seafarers have died in strikes on Black Sea shipping in recent months along with seven Azerbaijani crew members since June. On Saturday, a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged ship in a port in the Odesa region killed a crew member. Ukraine, for its part, has targeted tankers it links to Russia’s shadow fleet since July.

The energy war is also being felt in global markets. Ukraine reported more than 194 drone attacks on Russian refineries this year, hitting all 11 of the largest. Bloomberg News estimated that Russia’s fuel output has fallen by more than 30 percent. With Middle East supply already down as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran, global diesel markets are more exposed to the loss of Russian supplies.

Maximilian Hess, a nonresident senior fellow in the Eurasia Program at the Foreign Policy Research Institute, said energy is at least as important as grain in driving the diplomatic efforts. He pointed to a “clear frustration” among many countries over high oil prices, which reflect both the Russia-Ukraine war and the crisis in the Middle East.

“Of course, Ukrainian grain is important for them, but the oil-price factor is important there as well,” he told Al Jazeera. “I think it is those commodity-shock concerns that are pushing them to re-embrace this rhetoric, rather than anything else.”

Every previous attempt at diplomacy has failed to end the Russia-Ukraine war. A US-brokered, 30-day energy truce in early 2025 collapsed amid accusations of violations on both sides. At talks in Istanbul in May 2025, Zelenskyy complained that Russia had sent a junior delegation with no authority to sign a ceasefire.

In August 2025, a meeting between Trump and Putin in Alaska yielded no results despite Trump claiming to be close to a deal ahead of it.

Wesslau said Washington’s efforts have faltered partly because Trump – who had boasted he would end the war within 24 hours of taking office in January 2025 – has appeared unwilling to put real pressure on Moscow. “The Russians see this, and they conclude that they can continue this war,” he said.

Deep distrust remains. Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee, said: “Putin never keeps agreements.”

Moscow’s actions on the ground suggest it is in no hurry, Wesslau said “They’re trying to strangle Ukraine, strangle the economy, and make it unliveable ahead of the winter,” he said. He added that Moscow’s occasionally softer rhetoric was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and “has always proved to be a bluff”.

Russia’s terms are another obstacle. Hess said Moscow’s demands have not softened at any point since it launched the war and at times have grown. Putin has demanded all of Ukraine’s Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson and Zaporizhia regions, including territory Russian forces have never controlled, as well as a buffer zone in northern Ukraine. Moscow is also seeking sanctions relief and military concessions for any Black Sea deal.

“I don’t think it’s a question of who actually mediates. I think it’s really a question of the calculation in Moscow,” Wesslau said. “Fundamentally, the problem is that Putin doesn’t want a ceasefire or a peace agreement. He wants to continue the war. He believes that he can win.”

Analysts said only greater economic pressure is likely to change that calculation.

Wesslau said if Europe can close down Russia’s shadow fleet of oil tankers, “this would be a massive blow to Russia’s war economy.” Hess said the country best placed to shift things quickly is China, rather than the US, by cutting its purchases of Russian oil. However, he added: “I don’t think Beijing is interested in doing so.”

Hess said that unless there is an outside shock, the war “is much more likely to last another four years than another four months”.

articles.title: Bechi: Teacher who sexually abused pupil back in Indonesia jail after BBC investigation
articles.summary: Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani had been secretly released on parole in 2025, after serving less than half his sentence.
articles.body:
A former teacher who sexually assaulted a student has been returned to jail in Indonesia after a BBC investigation revealed he was secretly released early.

Mochamad Subchi Azal Tsani, known as Bechi, was sentenced to seven years in prison in 2022 after being convicted of sexually assaulting a female student at his father's prominent Islamic boarding school in East Java, where he worked as a teacher.

A BBC Eye undercover investigation revealed he was secretly released on parole in August 2025, after serving less than half his sentence. The woman he had been convicted of assaulting had not been informed - despite her legal right to know.

On hearing he was back in prison, she cried with relief.

"I pray that this doesn't happen to anyone else and that, going forward, the law will be applied justly in Indonesia," the former student, who wished to remain anonymous, told the BBC.

The Ministry of Immigration and Corrections previously told the BBC that Bechi was released because of sentence reductions granted in accordance with regulations.

But the BBC investigation sparked a public outcry and led to calls from lawmakers for an investigation, after which the government announced a comprehensive review.

That review found "errors" resulting in Bechi's parole being revoked. He has now been returned to prison.

Immigration and Corrections Minister Agus Andrianto told the BBC that those responsible for approving Bechi's parole "will certainly face sanctions".

"We want to make sure that such mistakes or irregularities do not happen again," he said.

For Ira Puspitasari, one of several former students who accused Bechi of sexual abuse and testified at his trial, the decision is a vindication.

"I'm amazed, really. I didn't expect the government would pay such detailed attention to this case and really pay attention to us, the victims," she said.

Ira, who has waived her legal right to anonymity, told the BBC she was raped and sexually abused by Bechi for more than four years, from the age of 15.

"I was treated as his slave. I was held captive, raped, beaten," she said.

She said she tried to run away but Bechi's private security guards tracked her down, kidnapped her and took her to a secluded hut, where Bechi tortured and raped her.

She said she reported all of this to the police but was then intimidated into withdrawing her complaint. She also shared an audio recording of Bechi's mother telling her to say that "nothing had happened".

Outside the UK, you can watch Catching My Teacher on YouTube .

Watching BBC undercover footage of Bechi smiling and greeting supporters at an event in March, when he should still have been in prison, Ira became tearful.

"It's like nothing ever happened," she said.

Ira was invited to a parliamentary hearing this week into the state's handling of sexual abuse cases in religious and educational institutions, held in response to the BBC's investigation.

Lawyer Joko Jumadi, who has represented several victims of abuse in educational institutions, also addressed the hearing and said authorities were often reluctant to investigate allegations of abuse because they involved "influential religious figures who have large followings".

He told the hearing that he regularly faced threats and intimidation as a result of taking on such cases.

Bechi is the son of prominent Islamic cleric Muhammad Mukhtar Mu'thi, founder of the Shiddiqiyyah Islamic boarding school in Jombang, East Java.

He was arrested in 2022 after a 15-hour police siege at the school, where supporters had gathered to prevent his arrest.

Prosecutors had sought a longer sentence after Bechi was accused of rape by a number of students, but he was acquitted of the rape charges and convicted of the lesser sexual assault offence of one student.

The BBC sought comment from Bechi, his mother and the Shiddiqiyyah boarding school as part of its investigation but received no response.

articles.title: UK’s Burnham ‘open’ to Germany joining GCAP fighter jet programme
articles.summary: GCAP pact between the UK, Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet welcomed Canada as an ‘observer’ in July
articles.body:
Prime ⁠⁠Minister Andy Burnham says the United Kingdom is open to Germany ⁠⁠joining the GCAP programme, a partnership with ⁠⁠Italy and Japan to build a new fighter jet, after meeting Chancellor Friedrich ‌‌Merz in Berlin.

“I’ve indicated to the Chancellor … our openness to Germany joining GCAP,” Burnham told a news conference on Thursday.

“That is something ⁠⁠that we seek ⁠⁠to progress in the coming period, working with our other partners, Italy ⁠⁠and Japan.”

There has been growing speculation that the ⁠⁠founding countries of the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) could open the door to ‌‌Germany after a rival Franco-German fighter programme collapsed in ‌‌June.

The GCAP pact to build a sixth generation fighter jet welcomed Canada as an “observer nation” in July.

As western nations seek to maintain air superiority over rival powers, the new warplanes will be equipped with AI, next-generation sensors and other technology.

Burnham is on his first official visit to Germany since becoming Britain’s prime minister in July. The leaders are also expected to confirm a new UK-Germany joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyberattacks and other hybrid threats from adversaries.

“Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat. They reach into people’s homes and workplaces and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided,” Burnham said in a statement ahead of the visit.

Burnham’s office singled out the threat posed by Russia in a statement on Thursday, but stressed that the partnership would confront security threats regardless of their origin.

As part of the agreement, the UK and Germany will share security information and work together to monitor, deter and disrupt threats.

British MPs have raised concerns in recent months about the potential threats posed by Russia, with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warning last month that Russia and its President, Vladimir Putin, were the biggest threat to the country’s security.

Germany has also raised concerns about what it sees as a growing security threat posed by Moscow. Last month, Berlin accused Russia of being behind a failed drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Moscow denies any wrongdoing.

Reporting from Berlin, Al Jazeera’s Dominic Kane said the security partnership is “supposed to send a message to several countries” about the intention to increase European security.

“It’s a way of demonstrating German and British intent in so far as Ukraine is concerned, but also more broadly about where Europe goes next, remembering of course that the United States plays a role in so far as NATO is concerned,” Kane said.

“We know that Merz and Starmer [Burnham’s predecessor] and we can assume Burnham want to show to the Americans, as much as to the Russians, how much European security means to them.”

Burnham and Merz are also expected to discuss other key issues for Europe, including ongoing support for Ukraine in its war against Russia and disruption to global trade routes, including through the Strait of Hormuz.

The leaders are also expected to formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty. The accord commits both countries to deepening cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and economic growth.

articles.title: M23 guerrilla war’s shadow economy: How Congo’s militias turn guns, gold and tolls into profit
articles.summary: In a remote mining village in the Democratic Republic of Congo, teenagers carrying Kalashnikovs guard a gold mine while claiming to fight for their
articles.body: In a remote mining village in the Democratic Republic of Congo, teenagers carrying Kalashnikovs guard a gold mine while claiming to fight for their country. But behind the language of patriotism lies another reality: a growing militia economy fuelled by war, mineral wealth, road tolls and ransom.Around 100 heavily armed militiamen now call the small village of Mwala in southeastern DRC home. Many came from South Kivu after government forces retreated following an offensive by the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group. They now provide "security" at an artisanal gold mine operated by a Chinese company and collect money from businesses and people moving through territory they control.The fighters call themselves "wazalendo", meaning "patriots" in Swahili, a name used for local militias supporting government forces against M23. Some say they are defending the country. Residents, however, say the militias are better known for extortion, while local officials warn that the proliferation of weapons could turn the region's unresolved conflicts into a larger security crisis.The development illustrates how the war in eastern Congo is creating space for armed groups beyond M23 to expand their influence, access weapons and profit from the mineral-rich region.How the M23 war gave militias a new lease of lifeThe M23 armed group controls large areas of eastern DRC and has played a major role in the violence and instability that has long plagued the mineral-rich region.But M23 is only one part of the security challenge facing the area. Numerous armed groups and militias operate across eastern Congo, complicating efforts to end the conflict between the government and M23.In December, M23 launched an offensive against Uvira in South Kivu province, triggering a chaotic withdrawal of government forces.As soldiers retreated, weapons, uniforms and ammunition were abandoned along roads. Some government troops were also forcibly disarmed by local militias that said they were prepared to fight in their place.Weapons and fighters subsequently moved into neighbouring Tanganyika province, which had only recently emerged from a brutal communal conflict.Since then, Mwala has become one of the places where these armed groups have entrenched themselves.Claude, the head of the Mwala militia group, said his fighters are paid between $100 and $150 a month to provide security at the village's artisanal gold mine."I joined the wazalendo self-defence force to defend my country," Claude said.He said he had been "at the front several times", while some of his fighters spoke of fighting in Minembwe, where some of the most intense clashes between government and M23 forces have taken place in recent months.But residents of Mwala told AFP by phone that they mainly encounter the militiamen as a source of pressure and extortion.From bows and arrows to machine gunsThe transformation of the militias is visible in the weapons they now carry.The Mwala militia operates from a collection of huts made from wood and foliage in dry scrubland. Young fighters pose with assault rifles when cameras arrive.Claude said the fighters had little support despite being involved in the conflict."We're hungry, we sleep badly, we buy the weapons and ammunition ourselves, all these efforts are ignored by our authorities," Claude said.Tanganyika is still dealing with the legacy of a violent conflict between Pygmy and Bantu communities that killed thousands between 2013 and 2019.Some militias have since been formally incorporated as auxiliaries of the Congolese army and are undergoing military training. Others, like Claude's group, have simply declared themselves "wazalendo".The return of large quantities of weapons has changed the character of the militias.Where village fighters once carried bows and arrows, several security and local sources say they now possess Cold War-era machine guns and even rocket launchers.Tresor Ngabo, representative of the national disarmament and reintegration programme in Tanganyika, said the development was particularly concerning because large sums of money had already been spent trying to end the region's earlier conflict."A lot of money has really been injected here since 2015 to put an end to the conflict. Unfortunately, the war against the M23 broke out," Ngabo said.Although the intercommunal violence ended seven years ago, he warned that conflicts had not disappeared."conflicts persist, but this time these people are well armed, and if there are new clashes, it will be chaotic," Ngabo warned.Gold mines become a source of militia incomeThe militias' influence is not limited to carrying weapons or fighting.They have also found ways to profit from the economic activity taking place in their territory.Chinese companies operate several mining operations in southeastern DRC, where the country's mineral wealth has attracted substantial foreign investment.In Mwala, the militia provides security at an artisanal gold mine operated by a Chinese company.But armed groups also impose charges on roads passing through territory they control.The Bishambuke militia, to which the Mwala group is affiliated, demands around $1,500 a month from companies travelling through its territory, according to a local mining operator.The group is also known for involvement in kidnappings of Chinese nationals for ransom.That combination of mining, road tolls and kidnapping has created a parallel source of income for armed groups operating outside direct government control.The result is a conflict economy in which controlling territory can provide access not only to weapons and recruits but also to valuable resources and businesses.Lithium brings fresh economic hopes, security risksThe stakes could become even higher as new mineral resources are discovered.Tanganyika has deposits of lithium, a mineral essential to electric vehicle batteries. Demand for lithium is expected to double by 2030, raising hopes that the resource could provide an economic boost to the province.But insecurity threatens those prospects.Foreign companies may be reluctant to invest in areas where armed groups operate freely, impose tolls and can target workers or businesses.China has invested heavily in the DRC over recent decades, and Chinese companies now operate many mining projects in the southeast.For local militias, the presence of valuable mining operations creates another potential source of revenue.The challenge for the government is therefore not only to defeat armed groups militarily, but also to prevent them from controlling the economic networks that allow them to survive.Army struggles to keep armed groups in checkMwala is only about 20 kilometres from Kalemie, the capital of Tanganyika province on the shores of Lake Tanganyika.By Congolese standards, the mining village is not particularly isolated. Yet the army, which has long faced accusations of poor equipment and indiscipline, has struggled to keep the militias under control.Some of the better-armed groups have even clashed with government troops.Kalemie is itself dealing with the economic consequences of the earlier communal conflict while absorbing tens of thousands of people displaced by fighting in South Kivu.At night, gunfire can still be heard in outlying neighbourhoods as heavily armed deserters break into homes and hold up residents.Operations by security forces have produced a relative lull recently, according to local authorities and civil society representatives.But the underlying problem remains. Chirac Issa, a civil society representative, said trust in government forces "has disappeared".He warned that the proliferation of armed groups in the province was a "time bomb"."Even if the war ends, would the government be able to collect all the weapons? The answer is 'no'," he said.The conflict could outlive the warThe spread of armed groups into Tanganyika shows how the consequences of the M23 conflict extend beyond the front lines in eastern Congo.A government offensive against M23, a peace agreement or even an end to major fighting would not automatically dismantle the networks that have emerged around the conflict.Some militias have acquired weapons abandoned by retreating soldiers. Others have gained access to mining sites, imposed road tolls or become involved in kidnapping.For communities already emerging from years of communal violence, the danger is that the weapons and financial incentives created by the latest conflict could sustain instability long after the main battlefields fall silent.In Mwala, the gold mine continues to operate under the watch of young men with assault rifles.For them, the war against M23 may be presented as a fight for the country. But for the communities living under their control, it has also become a business built around guns, gold and power.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: South Korea to recall Ukraine envoy in diplomatic row over POWs
articles.summary: South Korea recalls envoy from Kyiv amid diplomatic tensions over alleged transfer of North Korean soldiers to Seoul.
articles.body:
South Korea says it will recall its ambassador to Kyiv following a recent revelation by Ukraine of a transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement on Thursday came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologise over the revelation.

“The government has decided to recall its ambassador to Ukraine,” the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement.

“The government hopes that all outstanding issues between the two countries will be resolved amicably and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to that end.”

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his United Nations General Assembly address last month.

South Korea accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement relating to the transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers have expressed their desire to resettle in South Korea because they could face persecution if repatriated to North Korea.

South Korea had said it would accept them because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the nondisclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North.

There have been no comments from North Korea’s state media on the soldiers’ transfer. But the North has previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and its key ally, the United States, and focused on bolstering its nuclear programme since 2019.

South Korea has provided $445m in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100m in aid to Ukraine during a meeting with Zelenskyy.

articles.title: Fix infra before building high: Residents to Chandigarh administration
articles.summary: Chandigarh residents oppose Master Plan changes for taller, denser housing, urging infrastructure upgrades first over traffic, utilities, ecology and Shivalik views.
articles.body: Chandigarh: Chandigarh residents have sent a clear message on the proposed Master Plan amendments: build the infrastructure before building higher. Representations before the Screening Committee show strong resistance to denser and taller housing, with concerns ranging from traffic and parking to water, sewerage, ecology and the city’s low-rise character.While some stakeholders backed densification to meet housing needs and use land more efficiently, opposition was stronger to most major residential proposals.Group housing: Density meets resistanceOf 47 representations on residential amendments, 17 were unrelated to the notified changes, dealing with issues such as building violations, apartmentalisation and land pooling.For group housing in Phase II, including govt housing, three stakeholders supported higher density but wanted roads, sewerage, electricity and parking strengthened first. Sixteen objected, raising concerns that excluding stilt parking from building height calculations could lead to more dwelling units, residents and vehicles.The proposed stilt+4 format was also seen as inconsistent with Chandigarh’s low-rise, green character, with some fearing that taller buildings could affect views of the Shivaliks and undermine the city’s original planning principles.The pushback was stronger in Phase III. Three stakeholders supported higher density, but 24 objected to the proposed FAR increase from 1.2 to 3.0 and building heights of up to 98 ft 5 in.Traffic, parking, water and sewerage capacity, community facilities and environmental stress emerged as key concerns. Stakeholders also questioned how taller buildings would alter Chandigarh’s urban form and sought firm development limits.A few, however, sought greater flexibility, including retaining the one-acre minimum site requirement instead of three acres and allowing cooperative housing for govt, PSU and defence employees.Maloya: Residents wary of losing green edgeThe proposed residential development on 178 acres in Maloya drew one representation in support and 13 objections.The main concern was that high-density development could eat into the city’s green peripheral edge and ecological buffer and affect views of the Shivaliks. Stakeholders also cautioned against excessive urbanisation of the periphery and its possible social, environmental and regulatory implications under the Periphery Control Act.They wanted development parameters for Maloya specified in the Master Plan itself, rather than left to building rules, along with stronger parking norms for high-density projects.IT Habitat: Demand for ecological scrutinyThe proposed plotted development in IT Habitat received one representation in support and four objections.Stakeholders questioned the shift towards plotted development when earlier planning approaches had favoured higher-density development in peripheral sectors. One concern was that housing should primarily meet the needs of IT Park employees rather than become a general residential development.They also sought a proper ecological assessment and formal MoEF&CC clearance before development.Manimajra: Height without capacity a concernThe proposed stilt+5 group housing in Manimajra also faced resistance. The Expert Committee, headed by the deputy commissioner, had recommended the development subject to augmentation of water supply, sewerage, drainage, electricity, solid-waste management and public parking after a technical assessment.Of the 47 representations in this category, 37 were outside the scope of the notified amendments. Among those relevant to the proposal, one supported it while nine objected.The concern was straightforward: Manimajra is already congested, and adding height without first establishing adequate infrastructure capacity could intensify traffic, parking, sewerage and utility problems.Proposals await nodThe Screening Committee’s report, submitted to the UT chief secretary, records strong concerns from residents over taller buildings, higher density, peripheral development, infrastructure capacity and Chandigarh’s heritage character. The Chandigarh Heritage Conservation Committee (CHCC) has since cleared the amendments, but the proposals are still awaiting approval from the competent authorities.‘Need to debate further’RK Garg, a city-based social activist, said, “When most of the stakeholders have raised objections and serious concerns over these proposed amendments, why is the administration still going ahead with them? articles.title: At the center of Russia’s plague scare, residents ‘don’t trust’ officials – but have little other choice
articles.summary: When the Siberian town of Shelekhov found itself at the center of global headlines over a plague scare, residents might have hoped to be the best informed.
articles.body: When the Siberian town of Shelekhov found itself at the center of global headlines over a plague scare, residents might have hoped to be the best informed. But Russians have long been accustomed to living with unanswered questions and opaque governance. So, while the sudden death of 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute, sparked concern around the world, residents of the quiet town 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk told CNN they knew little more than the news – and rumors – spreading fast online. Six days after the news broke – and with no official confirmation that Shipilova died of plague, amid calls from the World Health Organization and the United States for more information – the situation appears to have prompted both resignation and skepticism. One 36-year-old resident who only gave her name as Evgeniya told CNN everything feels “normal, as if nothing had happened.” She said she isn’t panicking, but said a friend who works as a pharmacist told her that people had been stocking up on antibiotics when rumors of plague emerged. Russia’s health and consumer watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said Shipilova died of a pneumonia of “unknown” origin. The agency downplayed suspicions that her illness was related to her work but rushed to isolate her contacts. While Russia has kept a tight lid on information, CNN has spoken with residents of Shelekhov – where Shipilova died in the hospital Friday – and the nearby cities of Irkutsk and Angarsk to gain a window into the events of recent days, and scoured official and unofficial media reports for clues. The locals asked to give only their first names for privacy reasons. Despite the Kremlin repeatedly urging people to rely only on updates from the agency, Evgeniya said most people she knows didn’t trust the public statements. “There is no official information, and we don’t trust it anyway. There are a lot of rumors, but what is actually happening remains unclear,” she added. ‘Everything is fine’ Others voiced greater trust in the official narrative. Ekaterina, 26, told CNN that “things are not bad at all” for her – and that she didn’t see any need for concern as everyone who had been in contact with the lab worker had been isolated. “People are not giving in to panic and are carrying on with their lives as usual,” she said. “It’s the 21st century now, and there is treatment for plague. This is not like coronavirus, which was something unknown to people. The outlook is much better. So, to sum it all up: Everything is fine. We are following safety measures and not giving in to the madness,” Ekaterina added. That said, a pharmacist in Irkutsk, also named Ekaterina, told CNN that on Saturday there had been a run on “masks, antiseptics, and tetracycline antibiotics” where she worked, with people stocking up “just in case.” “People were, of course, afraid of getting infected,” the 27-year-old said. “There is no panic now. It only lasted for one day. We are not seeing it anymore. Everything is just as quiet and calm.” Alina, 38, told CNN the situation is “ordinary” other than seeing increased coverage of the situation across social media platforms, which she dismissed as “panic and has nothing to do with reality.” An unnamed Russian clinician who spoke to independent news outlet Lyudi Baikala (“People of Baikal”), which has led the way on coverage of the case, was unconvinced, though, by the Russian health watchdog’s statement that the lab worker’s illness was “unrelated to her professional activities.” Citing the need for laboratory confirmation to take up to 10 days, he was quoted as saying, “it is impossible to definitively identify the pathogen just one day after the autopsy.” ‘A deadly virus’ Residents cited in Lyudi Baikala described measures authorities took to mitigate the spread of the unknown infection. They said that, on Friday night, three vehicles pulled to an apartment block believed to be where the deceased lab worker lived in Irkutsk. They said personnel wearing gas masks and orange suits emerged from the vehicles carrying several containers and began disinfecting the entrances. “The smell was unbearable and very acrid,” a resident of the building - a woman in her 40s – told the outlet. The team that arrived told residents they had been sent by the health watchdog. “We asked what had happened. (The personnel) told us: a young woman had died of a deadly virus, but they didn’t know anything else. They said, ‘We showed up for work, were told to go and disinfect the place, so we came and did it,’” the woman was quoted as saying. CNN cannot independently verify the account of disinfection at the apartment block. One voice highlighting the human tragedy behind the global headlines was that of the mother of the young lab worker who died. Svetlana Shipilova – who was also in quarantine in an Irkutsk hospital – told local media outlet Glubina that her daughter hasn’t been buried yet. “After all, who would bury her when we’re sitting here in detention? She was such a hard worker. A pure, such a pure soul,” she said. Ordinary Russians often demonstrate resilience in the face of pressure, and exhibit a resignation toward state-directed narratives that is part of a survival mindset, rather than tacit support. Yulia, 25, told CNN that people are “no longer surprised by anything,” adding: “Information is always limited. I think it’s like that in every region.” A resident of Irkutsk who was responding to coverage of the case on Telegram used dark humor to describe how Russians perceive the euphemistic language of official statements. “An explosion is a bang. A recession is negative growth. A crash is a hard landing. A fire is smoke. A retreat is a gesture of goodwill,” he commented. “The plague is pneumonia of unknown origin… Anyone who catches this pneumonia of unknown origin should wrap themselves in a sheet and crawl to the cemetery. But do it slowly, because the main thing is not to create problems for the authorities.”

articles.title: How the IAF's first Hawai Sepoys came into being: Their story dates back to 1932
articles.summary: When the Indian Air Force was taking shape in the late 1920s, the British administration faced a challenge.
articles.body: When the Indian Air Force was taking shape in the late 1920s, the British administration faced a challenge.While six Indian cadets were to be sent to the Royal Air Force College at Cranwell for pilot training, the new force also needed Indian mechanics to maintain and service its aircraft.According to a historical account shared by the Indian Air Force on X in 2023, training a qualified aircraft mechanic under the prevailing British system took five years.But the new recruits had barely two to three years before the pilots were expected to return. The RAF initially looked to the Ishapore Rifle Factory for trained mechanics and later turned to the Indian Railways.The mechanics were to undergo training at the RAF Aircraft Depot in Karachi, learning how aircraft worked and how to maintain them. The RAF also planned to retain experienced British personnel to train and guide the Indian recruits.Even their designation became a matter of discussion. According to the IAF, British officials felt that using the rank of "Sepoy" could create confusion with the Army. In 1932, the ranks were renamed to give the new air force personnel a distinct identity. This was how the rank of 'Hawai Sepoy' came into being.When the IAF's first operational flight took place from Karachi on April 1, 1933, 19 Hawai Sepoys formed part of the small unit alongside six RAF-trained officers and four Westland Wapiti biplanes.Among the best-known Hawai Sepoys was Harjinder Singh, who later became an officer in 1942, earned his pilot's wings in 1950 and eventually retired as an Air Vice Marshal. According to the IAF's account, he also helped modify Westland Lysander aircraft with improvised bomb racks for operations against Japanese forces during World War II.

articles.title: California woman accused of spying for China fights detention with $820K in proposed security
articles.summary: Wanying Zhang offered over $800,000 in property equity for bail after her arrest while boarding a flight to China on unregistered agent charges.
articles.body: A California real estate agent accused of gathering intelligence on a relative of Taiwan's president for the Chinese government sought release from federal custody Wednesday, offering more than $800,000 in property equity and financial guarantees while disputing prosecutors' claims that she posed a flight risk. Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, argued through her attorney that her American citizenship, family ties and history of returning from overseas trips demonstrated she would appear for future court proceedings, according to a nine-page defense filing obtained by Fox News Digital. Zhang was arrested Sunday at Los Angeles International Airport while preparing to board a flight to China. She faces a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of a foreign government. FEDS SAY US CITIZEN GATHERED INFORMATION ON AMERICAN TARGETS FOR CHINESE COMMUNIST PARTY Her attorney, Craig Harbaugh, told the court that Zhang came to the United States in 2014, became a naturalized citizen in 2020 and has worked in Orange County real estate for approximately a decade. She lives with her husband and their two daughters, ages 8 and 5, according to the filing. The defense proposed using an Irvine residence with at least $700,000 in equity to secure her release, along with $120,000 in financial guarantees from her husband, his sister, his father and a family friend. Harbaugh also proposed GPS-monitored home detention, surrendering travel documents, electronic-device monitoring and restrictions on entering airports or contacting individuals connected to the case. The defense acknowledged that Pretrial Services recommended detention over concerns about Zhang's potential failure to appear in court, but argued that strict release conditions would adequately address those concerns. Zhang's lawyers also disputed the significance of her one-way ticket to China, arguing that she frequently booked international trips using separately purchased outbound and return flights. According to the filing, Zhang had traveled to China, France and Japan during the past year and returned to the United States after each trip. The defense said her planned October trip was intended to visit her mother and had been postponed until after her daughters' birthdays. TAIWAN ANALYSTS SAY TRUMP-XI SUMMIT PRODUCED NO POLICY SHIFT BUT REAL TEST LIES AHEAD The underlying criminal complaint alleges Zhang participated in a September 2025 surveillance operation outside the Seattle-area residence of a close relative of a Taiwanese government official. According to an FBI affidavit, investigators reviewed security-camera footage allegedly showing Zhang and another individual photographing the person and family members near their home. Federal authorities also alleged that Zhang transmitted photographs, video and vehicle information to a suspected Chinese government official through electronic communications. Investigators said Zhang attended China's University of International Relations in Beijing, which the FBI described as closely associated with China's intelligence apparatus. Zhang's attorneys contest the charge and maintain that she intends to establish her innocence. articles.title: Air India Delhi-Riyadh flight returns after Houthi attack on Saudi airport
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: An Air India flight from Delhi to Riyadh is currently returning to Delhi after Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia left one person dead
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Air India flight from Delhi to Riyadh is currently returning to Delhi after Houthi attacks on airports in Saudi Arabia left one person dead and eight injured, according to the latest information.Air India and Air India Express have suspended their operations to and from Riyadh until October 10, 2026, PTI rported citing Air India officials.Air India flight AI2243 had departed from Delhi and was flying south, over Gujarat, before proceeding over the Arabian Sea. The pilots subsequently turned the aircraft around and are currently flying back towards Delhi.The turnaround comes amid heightened concerns over safety in Saudi airspace following Houthi attacks targeting airports in the country, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.In a separate attack on King Khalid International Airport, one person was killed and eight others were injured, according to Saudi authorities cited by the BBC. The attack was among a series of strikes on Saudi airports over October 6 and 7.The Houthi group has claimed responsibility for the attacks, with its military spokesperson Yahya Saree saying the group targeted Saudi airports using ballistic missiles and drones.India on Thursday condemned the attacks on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, calling the targeting of civilian infrastructure “completely unacceptable”.“India condemns the attacks over the past few days targeting Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, which have resulted in civilian deaths and injuries,” the MEA said.“The targeting of civilian infrastructure is completely unacceptable. We express our deepest condolences to the families of those who have lost their loved ones. We wish speedy recovery for those injured. We express solidarity and stand with the people and government of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” it added.According to Saudi authorities cited by the BBC, attacks on the two airports over two days killed three people and injured 36 others. Two people were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on Abha International Airport, while one person was killed and eight injured in the attack on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.The latest attacks come amid renewed fighting between Saudi-backed government forces and the Iran-aligned Houthi group in Yemen.Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the attacks were carried out in “response to the Saudi aggression against our country”, claiming that Saudi Arabia had conducted “60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours”.The Houthi group also issued a “last warning” to global airlines operating flights through Saudi airspace, saying the area had become a “theater for our military operations”.Saree claimed that a ballistic missile targeting King Khalid International Airport “struck its target with precision and caused the disruption of airport operations.”“We reiterate our call and warning "for the last time" to all global airlines regarding the consequences of continuing to operate flights in Saudi airspace, which has become a theater for our military operations,” Saree said.He added that airspace over the “sacred areas” in Mecca and Medina was exempt from the warning.The US Mission in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday also urged American citizens to exercise heightened vigilance amid the Houthi threats, warning that the situation could lead to flight cancellations, airspace closures and other travel disruptions.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Centre to unveil AI regulation roadmap within a month; industry to shoulder safety responsibility
articles.summary: New Delhi: The Centre will release a consultation paper within a month to lay the groundwork for India's next set of artificial intelligence (AI)
articles.body: New Delhi: The Centre will release a consultation paper within a month to lay the groundwork for India's next set of artificial intelligence (AI) regulations, focusing on safety, human welfare, skilling, inclusivity and protection against emerging risks such as deepfakes and psychological harm.Announcing this at the launch of the World Bank's World Development Report 2026 on Thursday, electronics and IT minister Ashwini Vaishnaw said the government would adopt a techno-legal approach rather than rely solely on legislation, with industry expected to shoulder the primary responsibility for ensuring safety."Bulk of this regulation will have to be taken by the industries. Bulk of the responsibility will have to be taken by the industry," he said, flagging cybersecurity, deepfakes and psychological harm as major concerns.The minister also announced the next phase of India's AI computing infrastructure expansion, with the government initiating long-term procurement of 10,000 graphics processing units (GPUs), including an initial tender for 5,000. The proposed procurement arrangement would provide demand visibility for five years.In another development, Vaishnaw said India now has a visible three-to-four-year roadmap for developing indigenous GPUs capable of running AI models, particularly for inference. Further details would be announced in the coming months.The government will also empanel AI models and solutions for official use, allowing selected companies and startups to subsequently compete for departmental contracts.Emphasising wider access to AI, Vaishnaw said its benefits must extend beyond large technology companies to farmers, students, researchers and small businesses.Get the latest India News and Live updates.
